title: Woodrow Wilson's stroke, 1919 — and Edith Wilson's 'stewardship'
sources: Wikipedia: Woodrow Wilson — barnstormed the Western states to bolster support for ratification of the treaty and the League of Nations, returned to the White House in late September due to health problems; on October 2, 1919, suffered a serious stroke, paralyzed on his left side, with only partial vision in the right eye; his inner circle concealed the severity; awarded the 1919 Nobel Peace Prize on December 10, 1920 for his role as founder of the League of Nations; President Harding and the Republican Congress repudiated membership in the League

Wikipedia: Edith Wilson — Edith, his physician and a few close friends hid the true extent of his illness; she became the sole communication link between the President and his Cabinet and decided which matters were important enough to bring to him; her words: 'I, myself, never made a single decision... The only decision that was mine was what was important and what was not'; successfully pushed for the removal of Secretary of State Robert Lansing after he held Cabinet meetings without the President; historian Howard Markel: she 'was, essentially, the nation's chief executive' until March 1921
Wikipedia: Cary T. Grayson — the White House physician, involved in hiding the severity of the October 1919 stroke
Archive film (public domain, Wikimedia Commons): 'Woodrow Wilson video montage'; 'Video Clips of Woodrow Wilson (1917-1921, Part 1)' (US National Archives)

Photos (public domain): Woodrow and Edith Wilson at his desk, June 1920, Harris & Ewing — the first posed picture after his illness; Edith Wilson, Arnold Genthe; Wilson returning from Paris, July 1919; Robert Lansing, 1919; Dr. Cary Grayson, 1920

post.facebook:
On this day in 1919, President Woodrow Wilson suffered a serious stroke.

He had just toured the Western states to win support for his League of Nations, and came home to the White House with his health broken. The stroke left him paralysed on his left side, with only partial sight in his right eye.

His wife Edith, his doctor Cary Grayson and a few close friends hid how bad it was. Edith became the only link between the president and his Cabinet: every pressing matter was sent to her, and she decided what was important enough to bring to him. When Secretary of State Robert Lansing held Cabinet meetings without the president, she pushed for his removal.

She later wrote that she never made a single decision herself. The historian Howard Markel disagrees: she "was, essentially, the nation's chief executive" until Wilson's term ended in March 1921.

In December 1920, Wilson was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for founding the League of Nations. His own country never joined it.
